solution.concept_anchor: Strategic choice of salt as CDM symbol
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because salt's economic burden on the poor is a real and valid reason, leading students to stop there without recognising that the superior strategic reason was universality across ALL social groups, not just the poor.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): while the tax burdened the poor, framing salt's selection purely in economic terms for the poor understates its strategic genius — it also united the middle class and traders.
Eliminate (c): textile boycott was part of the Non-Cooperation Movement; Gandhi deliberately chose a different, more universally accessible symbol for CDM.
Eliminate (d): land revenue was a grievance but affected only peasants with landholdings — it lacked universality across class and caste.
Confirm (b): salt was consumed by every Indian regardless of caste, class, region, or religion — this universality made it strategically superior to all other possible symbols.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the nuance between the economic rationale (salt tax hurt the poor) and the strategic rationale (salt was universally used, cutting across every social division). A student who has read only summaries will choose (a) because 'economic burden on the poor' is the most-cited reason in textbooks. The trap is that while both rationales are true, the defining strategic superiority of salt lay in its cross-cutting universality — it was the one commodity that united peasants, urban workers, merchants, and even upper-caste Hindus in a single grievance.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's selection of salt as the vehicle for civil disobedience was a masterstroke of political strategy, not merely an emotional choice.

• Option (a) — Incorrect as the complete answer: The economic burden of the salt tax on the poor was a real grievance, but focusing only on this misses why salt outranked land revenue (which also burdened the poor) as a symbol.
• Option (b) — Correct: Salt was consumed by every Indian irrespective of caste, class, religion, or region. A Brahmin landlord and an untouchable labourer both needed salt. This universality meant that breaking the salt law was an act every Indian could participate in or identify with — no other grievance offered this breadth.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Textile boycott had been central to NCM; repeating it would have reduced CDM's distinctiveness and impacted Indian mill-workers too.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Land revenue grievance was real but geographically and socially limited to landholding peasants.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi wrote to Viceroy Irwin that the salt tax was "the most iniquitous" of all colonial imposts precisely because it hit the poorest hardest.
• The Boston Tea Party analogy — taxation on a daily necessity as colonial overreach — resonated internationally, especially in America.
• Gandhi compared the salt tax to taxing the air people breathe.

solution.concept_anchor: Gandhi's March 1930 letter to Irwin — content and context

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi's letter to Viceroy Irwin dated March 2, 1930 included a demand for the abolition of the salt tax among a list of eleven specific grievances.
statement_analysis.reason: The letter contained eleven demands, with abolition of the salt tax being one of them alongside reduction of land revenue, cuts in military expenditure, and other economic and political demands.

statement_analysis.statement: Irwin's receptive response to the letter delayed the launch of the Dandi March by several weeks as negotiations were attempted.
statement_analysis.reason: Irwin responded dismissively, refusing to engage with the demands, and this dismissal actually legitimized the march in public perception rather than delaying it.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 was a direct follow-up correspondence to the same March 1930 letter and constitutes a single negotiating continuum.
statement_analysis.reason: The March 1930 letter was an ultimatum before the march; the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 was a separate negotiated settlement arrived at after a full year of CDM — they are distinct events separated by the entire movement.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) tempts students who know Statement 1 is correct and assume Statement 3 is also correct because both involve Gandhi-Irwin correspondence, conflating the 1930 letter with the 1931 Pact as a single diplomatic thread.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Gandhi's March 2, 1930 letter did contain eleven demands including salt tax abolition — this is correct.
Eliminate any option including Statement 2: Irwin's response was dismissive, not receptive; there were no delay-inducing negotiations — Statement 2 is false.
Eliminate any option including Statement 3: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) is a separate event from the 1930 ultimatum letter — conflating them is the classic trap.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous trap here is Statement 3, which exploits a very common conflation between two Gandhi-Irwin communications: the March 2, 1930 ultimatum letter and the March 5, 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Both involve Gandhi, both involve Irwin, both are dated in March — yet they are separated by a full year and the entire CDM. Students who have memorised 'Gandhi wrote to Irwin' without distinguishing the two communications will accept Statement 3 as plausible and select an option that includes it.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's letter to Viceroy Irwin dated March 2, 1930 is one of the most significant documents in Indian nationalist history — a formal nonviolent ultimatum before civil disobedience.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The letter contained eleven demands covering economic, administrative, and political matters: abolition of the salt tax, 50% reduction in military expenditure, reform of the rupee-sterling exchange ratio, total prohibition, release of political prisoners, and others. Salt was one item in a broader indictment of colonial governance.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Irwin's response was dismissive. He expressed regret that Gandhi intended to break the law and offered no negotiation. This dismissal was politically significant — it validated Gandhi's position that constitutional redress was impossible and the march was morally necessary.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 5, 1931) was a separate negotiated agreement arrived at after a full year of CDM, not a continuation of the 1930 letter exchange.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi addressed Irwin as 'Dear Friend' — the salutation itself was a political statement of moral equality.
• The eleven demands were deliberately moderate, not demanding Purna Swaraj directly, to maximise participation.
• Irwin reportedly showed the letter to King George V, who questioned why Gandhi was not behind bars.

solution.concept_anchor: CDM demands vs. Purna Swaraj — deliberate moderation

statement_analysis.statement: The eleven demands presented by Gandhi before the Civil Disobedience Movement constituted a direct and explicit call for Purna Swaraj as resolved at the Lahore Congress of 1929.
statement_analysis.reason: The eleven demands were deliberately moderate — they focused on economic and administrative reforms such as the salt tax, land revenue reduction, and prohibition. Purna Swaraj was the Congress's ultimate goal but the CDM's stated demands stopped well short of explicitly demanding complete independence.

statement_analysis.statement: Jawaharlal Nehru, as Congress President during the launch phase of CDM, was in complete ideological alignment with Gandhi over the limited scope of the movement's demands.
statement_analysis.reason: Nehru harboured private reservations about the limited demands of CDM, which he felt fell short of the Purna Swaraj mandate he had championed at Lahore. His alignment with Gandhi was strategic and public, but ideological tension existed.

statement_analysis.statement: The Congress Socialist Party was formed during the peak of the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930 as an organised left-wing opposition to Gandhi's moderate strategy.
statement_analysis.reason: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934, after CDM had effectively ended — it was a product of the post-CDM crystallisation of the left wing, not a formation during the movement itself.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who correctly identify that Statement 1 is wrong (it is) and assume the other two must contain at least one correct statement — they then hesitate to choose 'all three are incorrect.'
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: CDM demands were moderate and reformist, not a direct call for Purna Swaraj — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Check Statement 2: Nehru had private reservations about CDM's limited scope; 'complete ideological alignment' is a scope-extension falsehood — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934, not during CDM in 1930 — Statement 3 is incorrect.
All three statements are incorrect — select option (b): 1, 2 and 3.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question traps candidates on two fronts simultaneously. First, the conflation of the Lahore Resolution's Purna Swaraj goal with CDM's stated demands — many students assume CDM was simply the 'action' phase of Purna Swaraj and therefore stated it directly. Second, the temporal trap on the Congress Socialist Party: '1930' sounds plausible because CDM was ongoing, but the CSP was a 1934 formation. Students who eliminate Statement 1 correctly often accept Statements 2 or 3 without verification.
solution.final_explanation:
CDM's strategic design involved deliberate moderation of stated demands even though the ultimate goal was Purna Swaraj — this was a conscious political calculation by Gandhi.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The eleven demands addressed specific economic grievances (salt tax, land revenue, military expenditure, rupee-sterling ratio) and administrative reforms. While Purna Swaraj was the Congress's declared goal since Lahore 1929, CDM's stated platform stopped short of explicitly demanding it — the moderation was intended to maximise participation across social groups.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Nehru's ideological tension with Gandhi over CDM's limited demands is well-documented. While Nehru publicly supported Gandhi and the movement, he privately felt the demands should have been more radical, consistent with the Purna Swaraj mandate he had championed.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934, after CDM ended — it emerged from the left-wing crystallisation that followed the movement's exhaustion, not during it.

Value Addition:
• The deliberate moderation of CDM demands also served a tactical legal purpose — specific demands could potentially be negotiated, giving Gandhi an exit ramp without appearing to capitulate.
• The tension between the Lahore mandate and CDM's limited demands foreshadowed the Congress left-right split of the late 1930s.
• Nehru's role as Congress President was largely ceremonial during this phase; operational decisions were Gandhi's.

solution.concept_anchor: Dandi March — date, route, and key facts

statement_analysis.statement: The Dandi March began on March 12, 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram.
statement_analysis.reason: Gandhi launched the march on March 12, 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad — this is precisely documented.

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on April 6, 1930, marking the formal commencement of civil disobedience.
statement_analysis.reason: After 24 days of marching covering approximately 385 km, Gandhi reached Dandi in Navsari district and picked up a lump of natural salt on April 6, 1930, symbolically breaking the Salt Act of 1882.

statement_analysis.statement: The 78 marchers chosen for the Dandi March were drawn exclusively from Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram and represented no deliberate regional or community diversity.
statement_analysis.reason: Gandhi deliberately selected 78 marchers to represent different regions and communities — the composition was intentionally diverse, not restricted to Sabarmati Ashram inmates.

statement_analysis.statement: Dandi is located in the Navsari district of Gujarat.
statement_analysis.reason: Dandi is a coastal village in Navsari district, Gujarat — the precise geographic identification is factually correct.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' tempts students who know the first two facts well and assume the third must also be correct since it sounds like a standard factual claim about the march.
elimination_logic: Verify pair 1: March 12, 1930 start from Sabarmati — correct, well-documented.
Verify pair 2: April 6, 1930 salt law broken at Dandi — correct; this is distinct from the March 12 start date.
Examine pair 3: the 78 marchers were deliberately chosen for diversity across regions and communities — the claim of 'exclusively Sabarmati Ashram' is false.
Verify pair 4: Dandi in Navsari district, Gujarat — correct.
Three of four pairs are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here targets the single most commonly confused fact about the Dandi March: the difference between March 12 (start date) and April 6 (the date the salt law was actually broken). Many students conflate these two dates. Additionally, the claim about the 78 marchers being 'exclusively Sabarmati Ashram' exploits the association between the ashram and the march — Gandhi actually selected marchers deliberately for regional and community representation, which was a key part of the movement's symbolic design.
solution.final_explanation:
The Dandi March's factual coordinates are precisely tested in UPSC Prelims — dates, geography, and organisational design all matter.

Consider the following pairs:

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| March commenced March 12, 1930 from Sabarmati | Correct |
| Salt law broken on April 6, 1930 at Dandi | Correct |
| 78 marchers exclusively from Sabarmati Ashram | Incorrect |
| Dandi in Navsari district, Gujarat | Correct |

Three pairs are correct; only the third is wrong.

Value Addition:
• The 24-day march covered approximately 385 km through over 40 villages — Gandhi addressed gatherings in each village.
• Gandhi was 61 years old when he undertook the march; the physical act of walking this distance added to its symbolic power.
• The number 78 was not arbitrary — it mirrored the number of satyagrahis who sailed to South Africa with Gandhi in his early resistance campaigns (though this is a popular but debated claim).

solution.concept_anchor: Parallel salt satyagrahas — leaders and locations
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps Sarojini Naidu and Abbas Tyabji for the Dharasana leadership, exploiting the fact that both led the Dharasana raid sequentially — candidates who know only Sarojini Naidu's name associate it with Dharasana without knowing Abbas Tyabji led first.
elimination_logic: Match A: Vedaranyam March — C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) led this parallel salt march in Tamil Nadu — confidently place A-3.
Match B: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan led the salt satyagraha in NWFP as part of his Khudai Khidmatgar movement — place B-4.
Match C: Abbas Tyabji led the Dharasana raid first after Gandhi's arrest on May 5, 1930 — place C-2.
Match D: Webb Miller was the American journalist whose eyewitness dispatch from Dharasana reached global newspapers — place D-1.
Correct combination is A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates at two levels. First, most students associate Dharasana only with Sarojini Naidu, not realising that Abbas Tyabji was the first leader of the Dharasana raid (arrested before he could reach the salt works), after which Sarojini Naidu took over. Second, students may confuse Webb Miller with an Indian journalist or political figure. Option (b) is designed to catch students who know Sarojini Naidu's connection to Dharasana but place her in List II item 2 without knowing Abbas Tyabji led first.
solution.final_explanation:
The CDM extended far beyond the Dandi March — parallel salt satyagrahas across India transformed it into a truly national movement.

Correct pairings:
• A (Vedaranyam March) — 3 (C. Rajagopalachari): Rajaji led a parallel salt march from Trichinopoly to Vedaranyam on the Tamil Nadu coast in April 1930, specifically to break the salt law in southern India.
• B (NWFP Salt Satyagraha) — 4 (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan): The 'Frontier Gandhi' mobilised the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts) in NWFP, demonstrating nonviolent resistance among Pashtuns — a remarkable challenge to colonial stereotypes.
• C (Dharasana Salt Works raid, first leader) — 2 (Abbas Tyabji): The 76-year-old former judge Abbas Tyabji led the Dharasana column after Gandhi's arrest; he was himself arrested before reaching the salt works, after which Sarojini Naidu assumed leadership.
• D (Eyewitness journalist, Dharasana) — 1 (Webb Miller): The American United Press correspondent Webb Miller's graphic dispatch describing the beatings at Dharasana reached over 1,300 newspapers globally, becoming the CDM's most powerful international publicity moment.

Value Addition:
• The Peshawar uprising (April 1930) saw Garhwal Rifle soldiers refuse orders to fire on unarmed crowds — a major moment of colonial military fracture.
• Rajaji's Vedaranyam March is sometimes called the 'Tamil Dandi March.'
• Sarojini Naidu's leadership of Dharasana made her one of the most internationally recognised figures of the CDM.

solution.concept_anchor: Webb Miller's Dharasana dispatch — international impact mechanism
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) traps students who correctly identify both A and R as true but do not examine whether R actually explains A — the international sympathy was generated by the nonviolent discipline of the resisters, not by Webb Miller's presence per se; Miller's dispatch was the medium, not the cause.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The Dharasana Salt Works raid became a major turning point in international perception of British colonialism — Yes, this is documented and correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Webb Miller, an American journalist, filed eyewitness reports from Dharasana that were published in newspapers across the United States and Europe — Yes, this is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Webb Miller's dispatch was the medium through which international audiences learned of Dharasana, but the actual cause of the international perception shift was the extraordinary nonviolent discipline displayed by the satyagrahis under brutal beatings. R identifies the channel (media coverage) rather than the underlying cause (nonviolent moral courage that made the coverage compelling). R is a contributing factor but not the correct causal explanation — it confuses medium with cause.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT correctly explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic 'both true but causally unconnected' assertion-reason trap. Most students, upon reading that both A and R are factually accurate, immediately select (a). The trap exploits a reversed-causation error: students assume that because Webb Miller's report came before the international sympathy, it caused it. But the report was the medium, not the cause — the cause was the extraordinary moral spectacle of unarmed Indians accepting beatings without retaliating. R describes a logistical fact (publication of dispatch) rather than the moral-political cause of the perception shift.
solution.final_explanation:
The Dharasana episode represents a critical convergence of nonviolent strategy and international media, and this question tests whether students understand the causal architecture.

Assertion (A): After Gandhi's arrest on May 5, 1930, the Dharasana Salt Works raid led by Abbas Tyabji and then Sarojini Naidu became a turning point in how the world perceived British colonial rule in India. This is correct — the imagery of unarmed satyagrahis being beaten with lathis without retaliating shocked global audiences.

Reason (R): Webb Miller, an American journalist, filed detailed eyewitness reports from Dharasana that were published in hundreds of newspapers across North America and Europe. This is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R correctly identifies the medium (Miller's dispatch) but not the cause of the perception shift. The international sympathy arose from the moral content of what Miller reported — the satyagrahis' extraordinary nonviolent discipline — not merely from the fact that a journalist was present. A journalist covering a violent riot would not have produced the same effect. The cause was the satyagraha's moral power; Miller's dispatch was its vehicle.

Value Addition:
• Miller's report is considered one of the earliest instances of mass-media-driven international human rights awareness.
• The Boston Tea Party parallel was frequently invoked in American press coverage — colonial taxation of a daily necessity.
• Sarojini Naidu's arrest during the Dharasana raid further amplified international attention.

solution.concept_anchor: CDM timeline — key events in sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places the Gandhi-Irwin Pact before Gandhi's arrest at Dandi (May 1930), which sounds plausible to students who remember the Pact was a 'compromise' without anchoring its exact date.
elimination_logic: Anchor Point 1: Gandhi's arrest on May 5, 1930 is fixed — this is after the Dandi March (April 6) and before the Pact.
Anchor Point 2: Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on March 5, 1931 — nearly a full year after the arrest.
Anchor Point 3: Second Round Table Conference was in late 1931 (September-December), after the Pact.
Anchor Point 4: CDM was relaunched in January 1932 after Gandhi's return from London and Willingdon's hardline posture.
Correct sequence: Gandhi's arrest (May 1930) → Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) → Second RTC (late 1931) → CDM relaunch (January 1932) — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here involves the Gandhi-Irwin Pact's exact positioning. Students know the Pact involved negotiation and compromise, which some associate with a period before active confrontation (i.e., before Gandhi's arrest). The correct sequence — arrest first, pact nearly a year later — requires knowing that the Pact came after a full year of CDM had exhausted both sides politically. Option (c) reverses the pact and arrest, the single most common sequencing error on this topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The CDM unfolded across three years with distinct phases — sequencing these correctly requires knowing not just the events but their exact annual anchors.

Correct sequence:
1. Gandhi arrested at Dandi (May 5, 1930): After breaking the salt law on April 6 and the Dharasana satyagraha following, Gandhi was arrested under Regulation XXV of 1827.
2. Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 5, 1931): After nearly a year of CDM, both sides negotiated — Congress suspended CDM; the colonial government released non-violent prisoners and granted coastal salt-making rights.
3. Second Round Table Conference (September–December 1931): Gandhi attended as sole Congress representative; the conference failed over communal award and independence deadlock.
4. CDM relaunched (January 1932): Gandhi returned from London; Viceroy Willingdon adopted a hardline posture and arrested Gandhi within hours — the second phase of CDM began under far harder conditions.

Wrong options fail by misplacing the Pact (before arrest) or placing the Second RTC before the Pact.

Value Addition:
• CDM formally ended in April 1934 when Gandhi withdrew the movement, not in 1931 at the Pact.
• The Communal Award (August 1932) was announced during the relaunched CDM phase.
• Willingdon replaced Irwin as Viceroy in April 1931 — the policy shift is as important as the timeline.

solution.concept_anchor: Women's participation — CDM greater than NCM
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) ('women played equally significant roles in both movements') is the most dangerous distractor because students who know women were active in NCM may equate the two levels of participation, missing the documented comparative difference.
elimination_logic: Identify the comparison: the question asks which historical pattern best explains why CDM saw qualitatively higher women's participation than the NCM.
Eliminate (a): women were active in NCM but CDM saw a demonstrable increase — 'equally significant' flattens a documented progression.

Eliminate (b): the claim that Gandhi excluded women from all CDM activities is factually wrong — he excluded them from the initial Dandi March but actively encouraged their participation throughout CDM thereafter.
Eliminate (d): women's participation in CDM was not limited to the domestic sphere — picketing liquor shops and foreign cloth shops were public acts of political resistance.

Confirm (c): CDM provided specific, tangible, public activities (picketing, salt-making, processions) that women could participate in from the public sphere — this represented a qualitative expansion beyond NCM's primarily domestic-sphere roles.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates in option (b), which exaggerates Gandhi's initial exclusion of women from the Dandi March into a blanket exclusion from CDM — a false generalisation. In reality, Gandhi's initial exclusion of women from the 78-person march was a tactical decision he later reversed, and CDM became the movement with the greatest women's participation in the nationalist struggle up to that point. Students who remember Gandhi's initial caution about women's inclusion may accept option (b) as broadly true.
solution.final_explanation:
A historian studying the records of women's participation in India's nationalist movements notices that CDM (1930–34) shows a significantly larger number of women participants than the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22). She is asked to identify the principle best explaining this difference.

The applicable historical principle is that CDM, unlike NCM, offered specific, visible, public acts of resistance — picketing foreign cloth shops and liquor shops, participating in salt satyagrahas, and joining processions — that women could engage in as public political actors. NCM had involved women primarily in spinning, wearing khadi, and domestic-sphere support roles.

• Option (a): 'Equally significant roles in both' — Incorrect. CDM saw a documented qualitative and quantitative expansion of women's participation.
• Option (b): 'Gandhi excluded women from CDM activities' — Incorrect. Gandhi excluded women only from the initial 78-person Dandi March; he subsequently and actively encouraged women's participation throughout CDM.
• Option (c): Correct. CDM's specific, tangible acts of public resistance created accessible entry points for women that NCM's more diffuse programme had not.
• Option (d): 'Limited to domestic sphere in CDM' — Incorrect. Picketing shops and participating in salt satyagrahas were distinctly public acts.

Value Addition:
• Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana raid — one of the most publicly visible acts of the entire CDM.
• Kamala Nehru and Kasturba Gandhi were both arrested during CDM.
• Gandhi's initial exclusion of women from the Dandi March was grounded in a paternalistic concern for their physical safety — a position he later reconsidered under pressure from women leaders.

(a) Women played equally significant roles in both movements, and the apparent difference is a result of uneven archival documentation rather than actual variation in participation
(b) Gandhi's deliberate policy of including women in all Civil Disobedience Movement activities from the outset ensured their greater participation, unlike during NCM where they were explicitly excluded
(c) CDM offered specific, tangible, and publicly visible acts of resistance — such as picketing shops and participating in salt satyagrahas — that enabled women to enter the political sphere in ways NCM's programme had not
(d) Women's participation in CDM remained largely confined to domestic support roles such as spinning and fund collection, similar to their NCM roles, but increased in absolute numbers due to the movement's longer duration

solution.concept_anchor: Frontier Gandhi — Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan identity
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Sarhadi Gandhi' is a strong distractor because it is another real title associated with Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan — students who know one epithet may reject it as 'odd' thinking only one nickname applies to him.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: the question asks which epithet/title does NOT belong to Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.
Verify (a): 'Frontier Gandhi' — this is Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's most famous epithet, coined because of his Gandhian nonviolent methods in the NWFP.
Verify (b): 'Sarhadi Gandhi' — Sarhadi is the Pashto/Urdu word for 'Frontier'; this is another authentic title for the same person.
Verify (c): 'Badshah Khan' — this is a common honorific used for Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, meaning 'King of Khans.'

Verify (d): 'Mahatma of NWFP' — this is NOT a historically documented or used title for Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan; 'Mahatma' as a political title was specifically associated with Gandhi and was not transferred as an epithet to Ghaffar Khan.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by placing three authentic titles of Ghaffar Khan alongside one plausible-sounding fabrication. 'Mahatma of NWFP' sounds authoritative because it combines two well-known elements — Mahatma (Gandhi's title) and NWFP (Ghaffar Khan's territory). A student who knows Ghaffar Khan well but has not specifically memorised the absence of this particular title may accept it as real. The three genuine titles ('Frontier Gandhi,' 'Sarhadi Gandhi,' 'Badshah Khan') are all documented.
solution.final_explanation:
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan was one of the most remarkable figures in the CDM — a Pashtun Muslim who built a nonviolent mass movement in the North-West Frontier Province.

• Option (a) 'Frontier Gandhi': Authentic. This epithet directly reflects his application of Gandhian nonviolence in the NWFP frontier region.
• Option (b) 'Sarhadi Gandhi': Authentic. 'Sarhad' means frontier/border in Pashto-Urdu; this is simply a regional-language version of the same title.
• Option (c) 'Badshah Khan': Authentic. A widely used honorific meaning 'King of Khans,' reflecting his stature among Pashtuns.
• Option (d) 'Mahatma of NWFP': NOT a documented historical title — this is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Ghaffar Khan founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) organisation, popularly called 'Red Shirts' for their red uniforms.
• The Peshawar uprising of April 1930 (during CDM) saw Garhwal Rifle soldiers refuse to fire on Khudai Khidmatgar protesters — a significant fracture in colonial military loyalty.
• Ghaffar Khan was imprisoned for over 15 years by the British — longer than any other major Congress-affiliated leader.

solution.concept_anchor: Gandhi-Irwin Pact terms — what it did and did not achieve

statement_analysis.statement: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 permitted Indians living on or near the coast to manufacture salt for personal use, but did not repeal the Salt Tax legislation entirely.
statement_analysis.reason: The Pact granted the right to make salt for personal consumption to those living on the coast, which was a symbolic concession — the full Salt Act of 1882 was not repealed, and the salt tax as a revenue measure continued.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact resulted in the permanent termination of the Civil Disobedience Movement, which was not relaunched thereafter.
statement_analysis.reason: The Pact led to a suspension of CDM, not its permanent termination. CDM was relaunched in January 1932 after Gandhi's return from the failed Second Round Table Conference and Viceroy Willingdon's hardline policy.

solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Both statements correct' attracts students who have memorised the Pact's salt concession without tracking that 'suspension' ≠ 'permanent termination,' a scope-extension error in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: the Pact granted coastal salt-making rights for personal use — correct; the Salt Act itself was not repealed — also correct. Statement 1 is accurate.
Verify Statement 2: 'permanent termination' — CDM was suspended, not permanently terminated; it was relaunched in January 1932 — Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 converts 'suspension' into 'permanent termination' — a single word change that completely alters the historical fact. Students who know the Pact ended active confrontation in 1931 may not recall that CDM was explicitly relaunched in January 1932, making 'permanent termination' factually wrong. This is one of the most tested CDM timeline errors in Prelims-pattern questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact is frequently tested on both its specific terms and on what it did NOT achieve — both dimensions appear here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: One of the Pact's key terms was the concession allowing people living on or near the coast to manufacture salt for personal use from seawater or natural sources. Critically, this was a partial and symbolic concession — the Salt Act of 1882 was not repealed, and the salt tax as a colonial revenue instrument continued. Congress accepted this limited gain.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Pact produced a suspension of CDM, not a permanent end. Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference (late 1931), which failed. Upon his return, Viceroy Willingdon adopted a hardline approach, and CDM was relaunched in January 1932. The movement formally ended only in April 1934.

Value Addition:
• The Pact did not secure an inquiry into police brutalities during CDM — a major criticism from Congress's left wing.
• The Pact also did not save Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev from execution (March 23, 1931) — Gandhi's inability to secure a reprieve was deeply controversial.
• Political prisoners convicted of violence were NOT released under the Pact — only those imprisoned for nonviolent CDM activities were freed.

solution.concept_anchor: Salt Act 1882 — legal basis for colonial salt monopoly
solution.strong_distractor: c — '1858' is a strong distractor because it is the year the Crown took over from the East India Company — students associate major colonial legislative moments with 1858 and may assume the salt monopoly was formalised then.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): the Salt Act of 1930 does not exist — there was no new salt legislation in that year; the 1930 movement challenged an existing law.
Eliminate (c): 1858 is the year of the Crown's assumption of India's administration — no Salt Act was enacted that year.
Eliminate (d): 1905 is associated with the Partition of Bengal — no salt legislation of significance dates to that year.
Confirm (a): the Salt Act of 1882 was the specific legislation that created the British salt monopoly and prohibited private manufacture — this is the law Gandhi broke in 1930.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places three plausible years around the correct answer. 1858 is particularly dangerous because it is strongly associated with major colonial legislative transitions. Students who know the salt monopoly was systematised by the British but cannot recall the specific year will often gravitate toward 1858 as a default 'major colonial legislation' year. The specificity of '1882' is precisely what UPSC Prelims tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal foundation of Gandhi's civil disobedience was a specific piece of colonial legislation — knowing its year is a testable precision fact.

• Option (a) — 1882: Correct. The Salt Act of 1882 was the statute that codified the British colonial salt monopoly, prohibited private manufacture, sale, or possession of salt, and made violation a criminal offence. It was this specific Act that Gandhi violated on April 6, 1930 at Dandi.
• Option (b) — 1930: Incorrect. No new Salt Act was enacted in 1930; the existing 1882 legislation was what CDM challenged.
• Option (c) — 1858: Incorrect. This year marks the transfer of India's governance from the East India Company to the Crown — no salt-specific legislation was enacted that year.
• Option (d) — 1905: Incorrect. This year is associated with the Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Movement — no salt legislation of consequence dates to 1905.

Value Addition:
• The salt monopoly's revenue significance lay in its regressive nature — it consumed a higher percentage of income for the poor than the wealthy.
• The Mughal empire also taxed salt, but the British systematised the monopoly far more rigorously through legislative architecture.
• After independence, India abolished the salt tax — one of the first post-independence legislative acts.

(c) Salt Act of 1858

solution.concept_anchor: Gandhi — Second RTC; Congress boycott of First RTC
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) pairing Gandhi with the First Round Table Conference is the classic UPSC trap — students know Gandhi attended an RTC but confuse which one, especially since the First RTC is historically more prominent in school-level discussions.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Gandhi did NOT attend the First Round Table Conference (November 1930 – January 1931) — Congress boycotted it entirely while CDM was active.
Confirm (b): Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference (September–December 1931) as the sole Congress representative, following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
Eliminate (c): the Third Round Table Conference (November–December 1932) was attended by only minor delegations — Congress boycotted it, and Gandhi was in jail during the relaunched CDM.
Eliminate (d): Ambedkar attended all three RTCs as a representative of the depressed classes — he was not the sole Congress representative at any of them.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a direct exploitation of the most common RTC confusion: which conference Gandhi attended. The First RTC is more prominent in Indian memory because it was the first major colonial constitutional consultation post-Simon Commission, but Congress — and Gandhi — boycotted it entirely. Gandhi's sole attendance at the Second RTC (as the sole Congress representative, no less) is the precise fact. Option (a) is designed to catch every student who knows 'Gandhi attended an RTC' without knowing which one.
solution.final_explanation:
The Round Table Conferences (1930, 1931, 1932) are a classic UPSC precision-testing arena — knowing which leader attended which conference is essential.

• Option (a) Gandhi — First Round Table Conference: Incorrect. Congress boycotted the First RTC (1930) while CDM was active and Gandhi was in jail.
• Option (b) Gandhi — Second Round Table Conference: Correct. Following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931), Gandhi attended the Second RTC (September–December 1931) as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress. The conference failed — the communal award deadlock and British refusal to concede independence prevented any agreement.
• Option (c) Gandhi — Third Round Table Conference: Incorrect. Congress boycotted the Third RTC (1932) and Gandhi was imprisoned during the relaunched CDM.
• Option (d) Ambedkar as sole Congress representative: Incorrect. Ambedkar attended all three RTCs as a representative of the depressed classes — he never represented Congress.

Value Addition:
• Ambedkar's clash with Gandhi at the Second RTC over separate electorates for depressed classes foreshadowed the Communal Award (1932) and the Poona Pact.
• The Second RTC also saw the presence of Muslim League representatives, princely state rulers, and various minority organisations.
• Gandhi famously declared at the Second RTC: 'Congress alone represents the whole of India.'

solution.concept_anchor: Social group responses to CDM — business class, minorities, NWFP

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian business class, including Marwari merchants, provided more active financial support to the Civil Disobedience Movement than they had during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
statement_analysis.reason: During NCM, the business class had been lukewarm, partly fearing economic disruption. By CDM, Indian industrialists and merchants — particularly Marwaris — had developed stronger nationalist consciousness and provided substantial financial backing to Congress and the movement.

statement_analysis.statement: Muslim participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement was uniformly absent across all regions of India, as the Muslim League and major Muslim political organisations formally opposed it.
statement_analysis.reason: Muslim participation was uneven, not uniformly absent. In the NWFP, the Khudai Khidmatgar movement under Ghaffar Khan brought significant Muslim Pashtun participation. The statement's scope-extension ('uniformly absent across all regions') makes it false.

statement_analysis.statement: The Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts) under Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan participated in the CDM despite the movement being predominantly Hindu in leadership, demonstrating the cross-religious appeal of Gandhian nonviolent methods.
statement_analysis.reason: Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgar — a Muslim Pashtun organisation — formally integrated with the Congress-led CDM, representing one of the movement's most striking examples of cross-religious and cross-ethnic nationalist solidarity.

solution.strong_distractor: b — '1 and 3 only' is the correct answer but students may select '2 and 3 only' if they accept the generalisation about Muslim absence as broadly true, knowing the Muslim League and Ali Brothers had distanced themselves from Congress.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: business class — especially Marwaris — gave stronger support in CDM than NCM — this is documented in nationalist historiography; Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2: 'uniformly absent across all regions' — the Khudai Khidmatgar in NWFP represents significant Muslim participation; 'uniformly absent' is a scope-extension falsehood; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Khudai Khidmatgar integration with CDM is well-documented; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the core trap. It contains a kernel of truth (the Muslim League stayed aloof, the Ali Brothers had departed from Congress) but uses 'uniformly absent across all regions' — a scope-extension that ignores the substantial Muslim Pashtun participation through Khudai Khidmatgar in NWFP. UPSC frequently tests whether candidates can distinguish between 'majority Muslim organisations stayed away' (true) and 'all Muslims across all regions were absent' (false).
solution.final_explanation:
The social coalition behind CDM was more complex than standard nationalist accounts suggest — business class support strengthened while minority participation was regionally varied.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Indian business class support for CDM was demonstrably stronger than during NCM. By 1930, Marwari merchants and industrialists had developed greater nationalist consciousness, partly due to the Great Depression's impact on Indian trade and partly due to the growing nationalist movement's credibility.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The qualifier 'uniformly absent across all regions' makes this false. Muslim participation was uneven — the Muslim League and most urban Muslim political organisations stayed aloof, and the Ali Brothers had broken with Congress. However, the NWFP saw massive Muslim participation through Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgar, and there was some Muslim participation in specific localities elsewhere.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgar formally affiliated with Congress and participated in CDM — their nonviolent discipline under British repression was remarkable and confounded colonial stereotypes about Pashtun militarism.

Value Addition:
• The Garhwal Rifles incident (April 1930, Peshawar) — Hindu soldiers refusing to fire on Muslim protesters — is one of the most striking moments of cross-community solidarity in CDM.
• Indian industrialists like G.D. Birla played a dual role: funding Congress while maintaining relations with the colonial government.
• The Ali Brothers (Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) had separated from Gandhi after the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation alliance collapsed in the early 1920s.

solution.concept_anchor: Poona Pact — reserved seats increased vs. Communal Award
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) claims the Poona Pact reduced the number of reserved seats for depressed classes compared to the Communal Award — this is the most widespread misconception; students assume Ambedkar made concessions that reduced his community's representation.
elimination_logic: Recall the Communal Award (August 1932): it granted separate electorates to depressed classes with a specific number of reserved seats in provincial legislatures.
Recall the Poona Pact (September 1932): Ambedkar agreed to abandon separate electorates in exchange for a larger number of reserved seats within joint electorates.
Eliminate (b): the Pact maintained joint electorates, not separate electorates — joint electorates were Ambedkar's concession to Gandhi.
Eliminate (c): reserved seats INCREASED under the Pact compared to the Communal Award — this is the counter-intuitive but correct fact.
Eliminate (d): the Pact was arrived at through negotiation between Gandhi (fasting in Yerawada Jail) and Ambedkar — it was not unilaterally imposed.
Confirm (a): the Poona Pact increased the number of reserved seats for depressed classes in provincial legislatures beyond what the Communal Award had stipulated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates through the widespread assumption that Ambedkar 'lost' in the Poona Pact because he surrendered separate electorates. Students apply a simple binary: separate electorates = Ambedkar's demand = good; joint electorates = Gandhi's demand = concession. What they miss is that Ambedkar extracted a significant compensation — a larger number of reserved seats within joint electorates — making the Pact a negotiated outcome, not a surrender. Option (c) encodes this common misconception.
solution.final_explanation:
The Poona Pact is one of the most misunderstood episodes in CDM-era history — students typically assume Ambedkar suffered a net loss, which is factually incorrect.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Poona Pact (September 26, 1932) resulted in an increase in the number of reserved seats for depressed classes in provincial legislatures compared to what the Communal Award had offered. Ambedkar agreed to abandon separate electorates in exchange for this expansion.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Pact maintained joint (not separate) electorates — surrendering separate electorates was Ambedkar's concession to Gandhi.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This encodes the most common misconception. Reserved seats were increased, not reduced.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Pact was a negotiated agreement, not an imposition. Gandhi's fast unto death created enormous pressure, but Ambedkar negotiated specific terms and signed as a contracting party.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's fast began on September 20, 1932 and ended on September 26 when the Pact was signed — six days.
• Ambedkar later wrote in 'What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables' that he signed under moral coercion.
• The Communal Award covered not just depressed classes but also Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, and Europeans — separate electorates for multiple communities.
• The Pact was among the first formal political agreements acknowledging depressed classes as a distinct political constituency.

solution.concept_anchor: Viceroy Irwin vs. Willingdon — policies and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact

statement_analysis.statement: Viceroy Willingdon signed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact in March 1931, reflecting the colonial government's pragmatic willingness to negotiate with the Congress leadership.
statement_analysis.reason: It was Viceroy Irwin, not Willingdon, who signed the Pact with Gandhi. Willingdon succeeded Irwin in April 1931 and adopted a far more hardline approach, ordering Gandhi's arrest upon his return from the Second RTC.

statement_analysis.statement: The British colonial government's initial response to the Dandi March was to dismiss it as a minor theatrical event, before escalating to mass arrests of over 60,000 participants as the movement spread.
statement_analysis.reason: The colonial administration initially dismissed the march ('Gandhi is making a nine days' wonder'), underestimating its political impact — an error they corrected with mass arrests as CDM spread nationally.

statement_analysis.statement: Viceroy Irwin adopted a hardline repressive approach toward the Civil Disobedience Movement throughout his tenure, refusing any negotiation with Congress leaders.
statement_analysis.reason: This describes Willingdon's approach, not Irwin's. Irwin was relatively pragmatic — he negotiated the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Willingdon, who replaced Irwin in April 1931, was the hardliner who arrested Gandhi immediately upon his return from London.

solution.strong_distractor: b — '2 only' attracts students who correctly identify Statement 2 as true and Statement 1 as false, but do not carefully check Statement 3 — which also describes Willingdon's approach attributed wrongly to Irwin.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Willingdon signed the Pact — false; it was Irwin who signed the March 1931 Pact; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Check Statement 2: dismissive initial response followed by mass arrests — this is documented; Statement 2 is correct, so it should NOT be in the answer for 'NOT correct' question.
Check Statement 3: Irwin adopted hardline approach refusing all negotiation — false; this describes Willingdon; Irwin negotiated the Pact; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both incorrect statements contain the same entity-swap error — Willingdon's characteristics attributed to Irwin and vice versa. UPSC frequently tests which Viceroy held which policy. Irwin was the 'pragmatist' who made the Pact; Willingdon was the 'hardliner' who arrested Gandhi on return from London. Students who know only that a Viceroy made the Pact (without anchoring the name) will confuse the two. Statement 3 is particularly dangerous — 'refusing any negotiation' sounds like strong colonial policy that students might attribute generically to any British Viceroy.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Viceroy Irwin and Viceroy Willingdon — in terms of policy and actions — is a classic UPSC entity-swap testing ground.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed by Viceroy Lord Irwin (Edward Wood) on March 5, 1931 — not by Willingdon. Irwin's relative pragmatism enabled the negotiation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The colonial administration's initial dismissal ('nine days' wonder') was a significant political miscalculation. As CDM spread nationally with Rajaji's Vedaranyam March, Ghaffar Khan's NWFP movement, and Dharasana, the government escalated to mass arrests — over 60,000 participants were eventually imprisoned.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This describes Willingdon, not Irwin. Lord Willingdon replaced Irwin in April 1931 and, when Gandhi returned from the failed Second RTC in December 1931, arrested him within hours — launching the relaunched CDM's repressive phase.

Value Addition:
• Irwin's pragmatism has been attributed partly to Labour Party pressure in Britain — the Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald was less hawkish on India.
• Willingdon's hardline approach included multiple special ordinances that effectively suspended civil liberties across provinces.
• The phrase 'nine days' wonder' (attributed to colonial officials) became a historical irony — CDM lasted four years.

solution.concept_anchor: Satyagraha — accepting punishment as constitutive, not passive resistance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Gandhi distinguished satyagraha from passive resistance AND that CDM involved accepting arrest may assume R explains A — missing that the willingness to accept punishment is a moral dimension that R does not mention, making R only partially explanatory.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Gandhi explicitly and repeatedly distinguished satyagraha from passive resistance, arguing that passive resistance is a weapon of the weak while satyagraha requires active moral courage and willingness to suffer — A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? The constructive programme (khadi, village industries, untouchability removal) was indeed an inseparable part of Gandhi's political resistance programme during CDM — R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The constructive programme explains Gandhi's vision of parallel social reconstruction alongside political resistance, but it does NOT explain the distinction between satyagraha and passive resistance. The distinguishing feature of satyagraha from passive resistance is the moral dimension of accepting punishment — this is not addressed by R. R is a true additional fact about Gandhi's CDM strategy but does not causally explain the assertion.
Both A and R correct but R does NOT explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the partial-truth trap: R is a completely true and important fact about Gandhi's CDM philosophy (the constructive programme was inseparable from political resistance). However, it does not explain WHY satyagraha differs from passive resistance — the explanation for A lies in the moral dimension of active courage and voluntary suffering, not in the constructive programme. Students who verify both A and R as true without testing the causal link will select (a). The trap is that R sounds like a philosophical statement about Gandhi's approach that could plausibly explain A.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's conceptual distinction between satyagraha and passive resistance is one of his most important philosophical contributions — and one that UPSC increasingly tests in its nuanced dimensions.

Assertion (A): Gandhi explicitly distinguished satyagraha from passive resistance. He argued that passive resistance is a weapon of the weak — it requires merely non-action or suffering without moral engagement. Satyagraha, by contrast, demands active moral courage: the satyagrahi must be willing to undergo suffering voluntarily, accept punishment for breaking unjust laws, and hold no hatred for the opponent. This is the constitutive distinction. (A) is correct.

Reason (R): The constructive programme — promotion of khadi, village industries, removal of untouchability, communal harmony — was indeed an inseparable part of Gandhi's resistance strategy during CDM. (R) is also correct.

Causal relationship: R describes a true feature of Gandhi's CDM framework but does not explain the specific distinction between satyagraha and passive resistance. That distinction rests on the moral requirement of active courage and acceptance of punishment — not on the constructive programme. Both A and R are correct, but R does not causally explain A.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi first articulated the distinction between satyagraha and passive resistance in 'Hind Swaraj' (1909).
• The constructive programme was Gandhi's way of asserting that political independence without social reform was meaningless.
• Accepting arrest (as Gandhi did on May 5, 1930) was a deliberate demonstration of satyagraha's moral logic: the unjust law, not the law-breaker, was on trial.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct

solution.concept_anchor: CDM vs NCM — key structural differences

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the Non-Cooperation Movement, which was withdrawn abruptly by Gandhi following the Chauri Chaura incident, CDM continued even after Gandhi's arrest in May 1930 because its decentralised structure enabled regional leaders to sustain it.
statement_analysis.reason: CDM's organisational design was more decentralised than NCM's — Gandhi's arrest did not paralyse it; the Dharasana raid, Rajaji's Vedaranyam March, and Ghaffar Khan's NWFP activities all continued without Gandhi's direct leadership.

statement_analysis.statement: The Civil Disobedience Movement had a specific, tangible law to violate (the Salt Act), which gave it focus and a concrete entry point for participation that the Non-Cooperation Movement lacked.
statement_analysis.reason: NCM was primarily a programme of withdrawals (from schools, courts, legislative councils) without a specific law to break. CDM centred on violating the Salt Act — a concrete, dramatic, universally relatable act of defiance.

statement_analysis.statement: The Non-Cooperation Movement received stronger financial support from the Indian business class than the Civil Disobedience Movement, making NCM better resourced at the national level.
statement_analysis.reason: The reverse is true — CDM received stronger business class support (especially from Marwari merchants) than NCM, where business class participation had been lukewarm due to fears of economic disruption.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement were launched with Purna Swaraj (complete independence) as their explicitly stated immediate demand.
statement_analysis.reason: NCM's stated demand was swaraj within one year (not Purna Swaraj specifically), and CDM's stated demands were the eleven reformist points — neither was launched with Purna Swaraj as the explicit immediate demand. Purna Swaraj was the Lahore Resolution goal but not the stated CDM demand.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' tempts students who accept statements 1, 2, and incorrectly validate statement 3 (mixing up which movement had stronger business support) while catching statement 4's error.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: CDM's decentralised continuation post-Gandhi's arrest — correct, evidenced by Dharasana and Vedaranyam continuing independently.
Verify Statement 2: specific law to break (Salt Act) giving CDM focus NCM lacked — correct; NCM was a withdrawal programme without a single law violation.
Check Statement 3: NCM had stronger business support than CDM — false; CDM had stronger business support; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Check Statement 4: both movements launched with Purna Swaraj as explicit immediate demand — false for both; CDM's stated demands were the eleven points, not Purna Swaraj directly.
Only two statements (1 and 2) are correct — select option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 reverses a documented historical fact — CDM had greater business class support than NCM. Students who know business support was a feature of nationalist movements but cannot recall which movement received more may accept Statement 3's reversal. Statement 4 exploits the Lahore Resolution connection — students who know 'Purna Swaraj was the Congress goal' may assume it was also CDM's stated immediate demand, missing the deliberate moderation of CDM's eleven demands.
solution.final_explanation:
The CDM-NCM comparison is among the most consistently tested themes in UPSC Modern History — knowing not just that they differ but precisely how and why.

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| CDM continued after Gandhi's arrest due to decentralised organisation | Correct |
| CDM had a specific tangible law to break; NCM did not | Correct |
| NCM had stronger business class support than CDM | Incorrect |
| Both movements explicitly stated Purna Swaraj as immediate demand | Incorrect |

Only two are correct.

Value Addition:
• The Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922) — where a mob burned a police station killing 22 officers — led Gandhi to withdraw NCM unilaterally, demonstrating the movement's centralised vulnerability.
• CDM's continuation after Gandhi's arrest was a deliberate organisational lesson drawn from NCM's vulnerability to top-level disruption.
• Purna Swaraj as a formal Congress resolution dates to December 1929 (Lahore); CDM's eleven demands were a deliberately moderate operational platform below that ultimate goal.

solution.concept_anchor: CDM historiography — schools and their key arguments
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps Subaltern Studies and the Cambridge School, which is the most common error since both are critical of simple nationalist narratives — students conflate 'criticism of Gandhian ideology' (Subaltern) with 'elite manipulation' (Cambridge).
elimination_logic: Match A (Nationalist historiography — CDM as high point of mass nationalism): Bipan Chandra is the foremost nationalist historian of CDM — A-1.
Match B (Subaltern Studies — peasant participation had autonomous motivations): Ranajit Guha founded Subaltern Studies; Shahid Amin's work on peasant consciousness fits here — B-3.
Match C (Cambridge/Revisionist School — elite manipulation for bargaining): Anil Seal and Gordon Johnson are the Cambridge School figures who argued CDM was elite manipulation — C-4.

Match D (Autonomous Pashtun motivation — Khudai Khidmatgar's independent agency): this fits the subaltern/regional agency perspective — but in this question it is matched to Webb Miller's international optics angle which is D-2.
Correct combination A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap between Subaltern Studies (Guha/Amin) and the Cambridge School (Seal/Johnson) is the most dangerous confusion in historiographical questions. Both schools critique simple nationalist narratives, but from opposite directions: Subaltern Studies argues that peasant participants had autonomous motivations NOT reducible to Gandhi's ideology (bottom-up complexity), while the Cambridge School argues CDM was elite manipulation of mass sentiment for bargaining leverage (top-down cynicism). Students who know both schools are 'critical' but cannot distinguish their critiques will swap them.
solution.final_explanation:
Historiographical debates on CDM have moved beyond nationalist celebration to encompass subaltern agency and revisionist critique — all three approaches appear in UPSC Mains and increasingly in Prelims.

Correct pairings:
• A (Nationalist view — CDM as high point of mass nationalism) — 1 (Bipan Chandra): Chandra's 'India's Struggle for Independence' celebrates CDM as a demonstration of Gandhi's political genius and the maturation of Indian mass nationalism.
• B (Subaltern Studies — autonomous peasant motivations) — 3 (Ranajit Guha/Shahid Amin): Subaltern historians argued that peasants and lower-class participants joined CDM for reasons (local grievances, religious interpretations of Gandhi) that were not reducible to Congress ideology — they had their own political consciousness.
• C (Cambridge/Revisionist School — elite bargaining) — 4 (Anil Seal/Gordon Johnson): The Cambridge School argued that CDM was essentially a tool for Congress elites to demonstrate mass support in order to strengthen their bargaining position with the British — not an autonomous nationalist upsurge.
• D (International media optics — global perception shift) — 2 (Webb Miller): The American journalist's dispatches represent the international dimension of CDM historiography — how the movement was perceived and reported globally.

Value Addition:
• Shahid Amin's essay 'Gandhi as Mahatma' (1984) is a landmark Subaltern Studies text on peasant interpretations of Gandhi.
• The Cambridge School's approach is also called 'elite conflict' model — it emphasises competition between Indian and British elites.
• Bipan Chandra's nationalist school has been criticised for underemphasising subaltern agency and communal tensions during CDM.

solution.concept_anchor: CDM two phases — 1930–31 and 1932–34 timeline

statement_analysis.statement: The Civil Disobedience Movement operated in two distinct phases — 1930–31 and 1932–34 — with the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 marking the suspension between the two phases.
statement_analysis.reason: CDM was launched in March 1930, suspended under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact in March 1931, relaunched in January 1932 after the Pact's breakdown, and formally concluded in April 1934 — two distinct phases separated by the Pact's suspension.

statement_analysis.statement: The second phase of CDM (1932–34) was more effective and better resourced than the first phase (1930–31) because organisational experience from the first phase had strengthened Congress's mobilisation capacity.
statement_analysis.reason: The second phase was demonstrably weaker — organisational exhaustion, withdrawal of business class support, reduced Muslim participation, internal Congress divisions, and Willingdon's hardline ordinances all combined to sap the movement's strength compared to the first phase's momentum.

solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Both statements correct' attracts students who accept Statement 1 (which is correct) and then apply a logical inference that 'experience from phase 1 must have strengthened phase 2' — which sounds plausible but is historically false.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: two phases of CDM separated by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact suspension — this is the established historical periodisation; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: second phase more effective than first — historically false; the second phase was weaker due to exhaustion, business withdrawal, and hardline repression; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates on Statement 2 through a plausible logical inference: 'more experience = greater effectiveness.' Students apply this general principle to conclude that the second CDM phase must have been stronger, without recalling the historical facts. The second phase (1932–34) was notably weaker — the business class had withdrawn support, Muslim participation had declined, and Willingdon's mass ordinances had pre-emptively disrupted Congress organisation. The 'experience advantage' assumption is logically intuitive but historically incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
CDM's two-phase structure is a precision-tested fact — most students know there were two phases but confuse their relative strength.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CDM is correctly periodised as two phases: Phase I (March 1930 – March 1931), culminating in the Gandhi-Irwin Pact's suspension; and Phase II (January 1932 – April 1934), relaunched after the Pact's breakdown. The March 1931 Pact marks the clear suspension between them.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Phase II was weaker than Phase I. The reasons for this weakening were multiple: organisational exhaustion from Phase I, withdrawal of financial support from the business class (who feared economic instability), reduced Muslim participation, the Congress left-right internal tensions, and most importantly, Viceroy Willingdon's preemptive mass ordinances that disrupted Congress organisation before Phase II could gain momentum.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi withdrew from personal satyagraha in May 1933 and CDM was formally ended in April 1934 — making the second phase two years of declining effectiveness.
• The Congress Socialist Party formed in 1934 was partly a response to the frustrations of Phase II's failure.
• Formal constitutional politics returned with the Government of India Act 1935, which followed the CDM's end — a product of the broader CDM-era political bargaining.

Salt as a Political Symbol: Strategic Choice by Gandhi

solution.concept_anchor: April 6, 1930 — date salt law broken at Dandi
solution.strong_distractor: b — March 12, 1930 is the most dangerous distractor because it is a real and important date in the Dandi March — it is the day the march began from Sabarmati. Students who have memorised 'the march began on March 12' may not have separately anchored the April 6 date of the actual salt law violation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): March 12, 1930 is the date the Dandi March began from Sabarmati Ashram — it is NOT the date Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi.
Eliminate (c): March 5, 1930 is not a significant CDM date; March 5, 1931 is the Gandhi-Irwin Pact — a completely different event.
Eliminate (d): April 13 is associated with the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) — not a CDM date.
Confirm (a): Gandhi reached Dandi after 24 days of marching (from March 12) and broke the salt law on April 6, 1930.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is the single most commonly confused date pair in the entire Dandi March narrative: March 12 (start of the march) and April 6 (breaking of the salt law). Both are real and significant dates. UPSC has tested this distinction in multiple question formats. A student who has only memorised 'the Dandi March, March 12, 1930' without separately anchoring April 6 will confidently and incorrectly choose option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Two dates define the Dandi March — and confusing them is the most common CDM error.

• Option (a) — April 6, 1930: Correct. After 24 days of marching from Sabarmati Ashram (started March 12), Gandhi reached the coastal village of Dandi in Navsari district and picked up a lump of natural salt, symbolically violating the Salt Act of 1882.
• Option (b) — March 12, 1930: Incorrect. This is the date the march began from Sabarmati Ashram — not the date the salt law was broken. A full 24 days and ~385 km of marching separated the start from the act of violation.
• Option (c) — March 5, 1930: Incorrect. March 5, 1931 is the Gandhi-Irwin Pact — a year later and a different event entirely.
• Option (d) — April 13, 1930: Incorrect. April 13 is historically associated with Jallianwala Bagh (1919); it has no CDM significance.

Value Addition:
• April 6 was also chosen deliberately — it was the anniversary of the Rowlatt Satyagraha (April 6, 1919), connecting CDM symbolically to India's first mass nonviolent resistance.
• Gandhi was arrested on the night of May 5–6, 1930 — a full month after breaking the salt law at Dandi.
• The phrase 'We shall now break the salt law' was Gandhi's declaration before picking up the salt — one of the most famous utterances in nationalist history.

solution.concept_anchor: Congress Socialist Party formation — 1934, not during CDM
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) places the Congress Socialist Party formation during CDM's active phase (between 1930 events), which is the most common error — students know it was formed 'in the CDM era' without anchoring the post-CDM 1934 date.
elimination_logic: Anchor the Lahore Resolution (Purna Swaraj) — December 1929, before CDM.
Anchor the Dandi March and start of CDM — March-April 1930.
Anchor the Gandhi-Irwin Pact — March 1931.
The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934, AFTER CDM formally ended in April 1934 — it is a post-CDM crystallisation of the left wing.
Correct sequence: Lahore Resolution (1929) → Dandi March/CDM launch (1930) → Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) → Congress Socialist Party formation (1934) — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the Congress Socialist Party's formation year. Students who know it was formed 'in the aftermath of CDM' may place it during the active CDM phase (1930–32) rather than after CDM's formal end in 1934. The critical distinction: CSP was formed in 1934 as a product of the post-CDM left-wing crystallisation, not as an opposition during the movement. Option (a) exploits this by placing the CSP between the Dandi March (1930) and the Pact (1931).
solution.final_explanation:
Sequencing Congress's organisational evolution requires distinguishing events within CDM from those in its aftermath.

Correct sequence:
1. Lahore Resolution on Purna Swaraj (December 1929): Congress declared complete independence as its goal — the political mandate that preceded CDM.
2. Dandi March and CDM launch (March–April 1930): Gandhi began the salt march, marking the commencement of organised civil disobedience.
3. Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931): CDM suspended; Congress agreed to participate in the Second Round Table Conference.
4. Congress Socialist Party formation (1934): After CDM's formal conclusion, the left wing of Congress — frustrated by the movement's limitations and the perceived moderation of Gandhi's approach — crystallised into the CSP under Jayaprakash Narayan and Acharya Narendra Deva.

Option (a) places CSP before the Pact — incorrect by three years. Options (b) and (d) further misarrange the sequence.

Value Addition:
• The CSP was founded in Patna in May 1934 — Jayaprakash Narayan was its first General Secretary.
• The CSP functioned as a party within Congress, not a breakaway — it pushed for socialist economic policies within the nationalist framework.
• Jawaharlal Nehru, though not a formal CSP member, was ideologically aligned with its goals.

solution.concept_anchor: Dharasana raid leaders — Abbas Tyabji first, Sarojini Naidu second
solution.strong_distractor: b — Pairing Sarojini Naidu with the Dharasana raid is factually correct but incomplete — she was the second leader after Abbas Tyabji. Students who know Sarojini Naidu's connection to Dharasana may confidently accept (b) without recognising it is correctly matched only partially, or may simply not know Abbas Tyabji led first.
elimination_logic: Check (a): C. Rajagopalachari — Dharasana Salt Works — incorrect; Rajaji led the Vedaranyam March in Tamil Nadu, not Dharasana.
Check (b): Sarojini Naidu — first leader of the Dharasana raid — incorrect; Sarojini Naidu was the second leader; Abbas Tyabji led first and was arrested before reaching the salt works.
Check (c): Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan — Vedaranyam March — incorrect; Ghaffar Khan led the NWFP salt satyagraha; Rajaji led Vedaranyam.

Check (d): Abbas Tyabji — first leader of the Dharasana Salt Works raid after Gandhi's arrest — correct; Tyabji, a 76-year-old former judge, led the Dharasana column first and was arrested on the way.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the widespread knowledge that Sarojini Naidu was associated with Dharasana without the precision that she was the second leader — Abbas Tyabji preceded her. Option (b) is the most dangerous distractor because Sarojini Naidu genuinely did lead the Dharasana raid, but only after Tyabji's arrest. The entity-swap between Rajaji and Ghaffar Khan (options a and c) provides additional traps for students who know regional leaders by name but not by specific event.
solution.final_explanation:
The leadership sequence of the Dharasana raid is one of the most precisely tested CDM facts — knowing the first leader (Tyabji) is rarer than knowing the more famous second leader (Naidu).

• Option (a): C. Rajagopalachari — Dharasana Salt Works: Incorrect. Rajaji led the Vedaranyam March in Tamil Nadu, a parallel salt satyagraha hundreds of miles away from Dharasana in Gujarat.
• Option (b): Sarojini Naidu — first leader of Dharasana raid: Incorrect. Naidu led the raid but was the second leader. Abbas Tyabji led the initial column; he was arrested before reaching the salt works, after which Naidu assumed command.
• Option (c): Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan — Vedaranyam March: Incorrect. Ghaffar Khan led the salt satyagraha in the North-West Frontier Province; Vedaranyam was Rajaji's march.
• Option (d): Abbas Tyabji — first leader of Dharasana raid: Correct. The 76-year-old former High Court judge Abbas Tyabji led the Dharasana column after Gandhi's arrest on May 5, 1930 — he was himself arrested before the column reached the salt works.

Value Addition:
• Sarojini Naidu, upon leading the Dharasana raid, reportedly said to the marchers: 'You must not use any violence under any circumstances. You will be beaten but you must not resist.'
• Webb Miller's account of the Dharasana beatings was printed in 1,300 newspapers worldwide.
• Abbas Tyabji was one of the oldest satyagrahis to lead a direct action in CDM — his participation carried powerful moral symbolism.
